content: Microbiology is the scientific study of microorganisms, which are microscopic organisms that can exist as single cells or cell clusters. These include eukaryotic organisms such as fungi and protists, as well as prokaryotic organisms like bacteria and certain algae. Viruses, although not classified as living organisms, are also studied within microbiology. This field encompasses various branches, including virology, mycology, parasitology, and others. Specialists in microbiology are referred to as microbiologists. Despite significant advancements in the field, it is estimated that only about 1% of all microbes on Earth have been studied. Therefore, even though over 300 years have passed since the discovery of microbes, microbiology remains in its early stages compared to other biological sciences like zoology, botany, and entomology. The existence of microorganisms was hypothesized during the late Middle Ages but was not observed or proven until the invention of the microscope in the 17th century. In 1020, Avicenna (Abū Alī ibn Sīnā) suggested in The Canon of Medicine that bodily secretions could be contaminated by foreign substances before causing infection, though he did not identify these as the primary cause of disease. During the Black Death in the 14th century, scholars like Ibn Khatima and Ibn al-Khatib proposed that infectious diseases were caused by microorganisms entering the human body. Bacteria were first observed in 1676 by Anton van Leeuwenhoek using a single-lens microscope of his own design. The term bacterium was introduced later, in 1828, by Ehrenberg, derived from the Greek word bakterion, meaning small stick. While van Leeuwenhoek is often credited as the first microbiologist, Robert Hooke made an earlier microbiological observation in 1665, describing the fruiting bodies of molds. The field of bacteriology, which later became a subdiscipline of microbiology, is considered to have been founded by Ferdinand Cohn, a botanist who studied algae and photosynthetic bacteria. Cohn described several bacteria, including Bacillus and Beggiatoa, and developed a taxonomic classification system for bacteria. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch, contemporaries of Cohn, are often regarded as the founders of medical microbiology. Pasteur is renowned for his experiments disproving the theory of spontaneous generation, solidifying microbiology as a biological science. He also developed methods for food preservation (pasteurization) and vaccines for diseases such as anthrax, fowl cholera, and rabies. Koch is best known for his contributions to the germ theory of disease, proving that specific diseases are caused by specific pathogenic microorganisms. He developed a set of criteria known as Koch's postulates and was among the first to isolate bacteria in pure culture, describing novel bacteria such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis. While Pasteur and Koch laid the foundation for microbiology, their work focused primarily on microorganisms with direct medical relevance, overlooking the broader diversity of the microbial world. The true scope of microbiology was revealed through the work of Martinus Beijerinck and Sergei Winogradsky, who are considered the founders of general microbiology. Beijerinck discovered viruses and developed enrichment culture techniques, enabling the cultivation of diverse microbes with varying physiologies. His work on the Tobacco Mosaic Virus established key principles of virology. Winogradsky introduced the concept of chemolithotrophy, highlighting the essential role of microorganisms in geochemical processes. He was the first to isolate and describe nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Microbiology can be divided into several subdisciplines: Microbial physiology focuses on the biochemical functioning of microbial cells, including their growth, metabolism, and cellular structure. Microbial genetics examines the organization and regulation of genes in microbes, closely related to molecular biology. Medical microbiology studies the role of microbes in human illness, including microbial pathogenesis and epidemiology, and is linked to pathology and immunology. Veterinary microbiology explores the role of microbes in animal health and veterinary medicine. Environmental microbiology investigates the function and diversity of microbes in natural environments, including microbial ecology, nutrient cycling, geomicrobiology, and bioremediation. It also characterizes microbial habitats such as the rhizosphere, phyllosphere, soil, groundwater, oceans, and extreme environments. Evolutionary microbiology studies the evolution, systematics, and taxonomy of microbes. Industrial microbiology involves the use of microbes in industrial processes, such as fermentation, wastewater treatment, and biotechnology applications like brewing and enzyme production. Aeromicrobiology examines airborne microorganisms. Food microbiology focuses on microbes that cause food spoilage. Pharmaceutical microbiology studies microorganisms that cause contamination and spoilage in pharmaceutical products. Microorganisms are also utilized in biotechnological applications, such as producing enzymes like Taq polymerase, developing genetic tools like reporter genes, and advancing molecular biology techniques like the yeast two-hybrid system. They play a critical role in microbial biodegradation and bioremediation of domestic, agricultural, and industrial wastes, as well as subsurface pollution in soils, sediments, and marine environments. The effectiveness of microbial biodegradation depends on the nature of the contaminants, and mixed bacterial species are often used to target multiple pollutant types. Additionally, probiotics (beneficial bacteria for the digestive system) and prebiotics (substances promoting the growth of probiotics) are believed to contribute to human and animal health.
